reference_reasoning:
The most coherent explanation is a cooperative surface-binding mode that increases lateral conformity while keeping the organic separation normal to the perovskite/C60 interface small. The common amidinium motif can passivate undercoordinated Pb/I-related surface defects, whereas appropriately positioned heteroaromatic N atoms can participate in additional Pb-centred interactions and redistribute charge over the Pb–I surface. A more surface-parallel, multipoint arrangement can therefore do two things that are usually in tension: cover/passivate more defective surface area and reduce the effective tunnelling distance to C60. That is consistent with higher QFLS, smaller ligand aggregates, more homogeneous surface potential and lower contact resistance without formation of a detectable 2D perovskite layer.

The strongest alternative is not “nothing happens”, but that L2/L3 simply leave a larger or more uniform retained population and/or a different interfacial dipole. Equal 1 mg mL−1 solutions are not equal molar doses and certainly not equal adsorbed areal densities. More complete coverage could suppress SRH loss, and the measured band-edge shift could improve contact energetics, without a unique topology change.

I would switch away from topology as the dominant mechanism if, after matching retained areal density, roughness/overlayer thickness and C60 energy offset, a genuinely orientation-sensitive observable showed little or no orientation difference while QFLS, electrical collection and series resistance still followed coverage or dipole. The converse is strongest support: orientation changes at matched coverage/energetics and the evaporated-C60 extraction response follows that change. Binding-energy or vibrational shifts alone are insufficient because they establish interaction, not a unique finite-temperature orientation distribution.
accepted_alternatives: A conformal multipoint-adsorption mechanism may be described without the word “planar” if it explicitly couples perovskite defect passivation to reduced effective organic thickness/electronic separation at C60.

Coverage/retained amount, ligand-induced dipole/energy-level alignment, or ligand-driven removal/redistribution of surface PbI2 are acceptable serious alternatives if the answer states how they can reproduce both passivation and contact trends.

A matched-dose/coverage experiment, orientation-sensitive NEXAFS/SFG/polarized vibrational measurement, or an equivalent crossed comparison that decouples orientation from energetic alignment is an acceptable decisive route.

A high-information intervention is a positional-isomer control that keeps the amidinium anchor, CF3 terminus, aromatic ring size, heteroatom count and overall molecular length as similar as practical, but relocates one ring N so that simultaneous surface contacts in the proposed low-height arrangement are geometrically frustrated. The point is not to make a “worse ligand”; it is to perturb the spatial relationship among donor sites while minimizing changes in composition. A steric lock that changes tilt at nearly fixed electronic structure is another valid implementation.

The comparison must be made at matched molar treatment and, more importantly, matched retained areal density/effective thickness. Surface Pb/I stoichiometry, residual PbI2, roughness and work-function/CBM shift should be quantified so that a coverage or dipole difference is not silently substituted for topology. An orientation-sensitive surface measurement should verify that the perturbation actually changed the molecular arrangement; interaction-sensitive XPS or FTIR alone is not enough.

On bare perovskite, the cleanest topology test need not require identical QFLS, because moving ring N can also alter passivation. However, if the common anchor still gives comparable QFLS at matched coverage while the geometry-frustrated analogue loses the fast, low-resistance response only after identical evaporated C60 deposition, the topology-to-coupling link is strongly supported. reference_reasoning:
Neither claim follows from TRPL alone. Before C60, the longer lifetime together with higher QFLS is consistent with suppressed non-radiative recombination in the emissive perovskite population. After C60 is added, electron transfer becomes an additional depopulation pathway, so productive extraction can shorten PL decay. But a newly created interfacial SRH channel would also shorten the decay. The contacted lifetime is therefore a competition among transfer, radiative recombination, trap-assisted loss, diffusion and possible interfacial accumulation; it is not itself a collected-current measurement.

A productive-transfer interpretation becomes convincing only when the short contacted decay is accompanied by an independent increase in extracted/collected charge or transient photocurrent, lower contact/series resistance, and no corresponding collapse of contact QFLS/VOC or recombination resistance. If the lifetime shortens while collected charge, QFLS/VOC or Rrec deteriorates, contact-induced non-radiative quenching is the stronger explanation. The reported biexponential decays also mean that inverse average lifetime cannot automatically be treated as a microscopic transfer rate without a population-resolved kinetic model.

The energy-level shift is a second confound, not a sufficient cause. Moving the perovskite CBM closer to C60 reduces the interfacial energy loss while retaining downhill electron transfer, but it does not identify whether the faster depopulation arises from improved electronic coupling/shorter separation or from the energetic change. The decisive pattern is a crossed comparison: at matched retained coverage and nearly matched CBM–C60 offset, verified changes in molecular arrangement/effective separation should still change extraction if coupling is causal; conversely, at similar geometry, changing the energetic offset should move extraction if dipole/alignment dominates. The inference should be made on evaporated-C60 contacts.
accepted_alternatives: Independent collection can be established by transient photocurrent, charge extraction, selective-contact transport/contact-resistance analysis or another calibrated electrical observable.
A global kinetic model combining TRPL with transient absorption or carrier-density-dependent measurements is acceptable in place of a simple lifetime argument.

Temperature-dependent or externally tuned energetic measurements can be used to separate coupling/distance from an activation/barrier picture, provided the answer states the assumptions and verifies that geometry/coverage did not also change.

reference_reasoning:
The wide-gap result establishes functional portability, not mechanistic identity. The higher VOC and PCE are consistent with reduced interfacial non-radiative loss in Cs0.22FA0.78Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3, but the Br-rich mixed-halide surface has different defect energetics, local termination and ionic/phase dynamics from the near-iodide normal-gap absorber. A treatment can improve initial QFLS/VOC while leaving illumination-driven halide redistribution or ion accumulation unchanged. Therefore the normal-gap adsorption mechanism cannot be assumed to transfer simply because the wide-gap J–V curve improves.

The ~14 cm² result shows that the chemistry is compatible with a substantially larger-area fabrication flow, but it is a different iodide-rich absorber and front-contact process. It therefore supports process scalability more strongly than mechanism conservation. Spatial nonuniformity can be hidden in a single module J–V number, so area-resolved luminescence/photovoltage and contact-resistance or current mapping are needed.

Likewise, the 258-day treated-module field record is valuable durability evidence for that module, but it is not a matched comparative lifetime experiment because the control is followed for only 27 days. I would advance the chemistry to tandem-relevant wide-gap modules only after matched treated/control modules are operated for the same MPP/thermal/light exposure and show stable VOC/FF plus spatially uniform extraction. For the mixed-halide absorber, operando or repeated PL/EL spectral mapping should show no treatment-induced enhancement of light-driven phase/halide redistribution; complementary before/after ion-sensitive or surface-potential mapping can test interfacial accumulation. A go decision requires the interfacial gain to persist without introducing a new composition-dependent degradation mode.
accepted_alternatives: Equivalent monitoring of mixed-halide phase/ionic stability using spatially and spectrally resolved PL/EL, operando absorption, XRD/GIWAXS under illumination, or before/after ion profiling is acceptable if it addresses the same causal risk.
Scale uniformity may be tested by PLQY/QFLS mapping, electroluminescence imaging, sheet/contact-resistance mapping, local JV or other area-resolved methods rather than any single named technique.

A conditional no-go decision is acceptable if it is tied to matched-duration degradation, growing spectral phase-segregation signatures, nonuniform contact extraction or loss of VOC/FF under operating stress.
